Web design is the process of planning, modelling and building content that people receive through the Internet. A web designer uses markup languages such as HTML, so that a web browser can interpret the content and show it on the screen.

The intent of web design is to create a web site: a collection of files stored on one or more web servers. When a user requests a page, the server sends it back, and the browser displays text, forms, pictures and interactive elements.

Simple elements are placed on a page with HTML tags. For example, bit-mapped images in GIF, JPEG or PNG format are added with the img tag. In the past, more complex media such as animation, video and sound required plug-ins like Flash or QuickTime. Plug-ins were also embedded into pages with tags.

Web design is a creative and technical process. Designers plan, model and build electronic content and deliver it through the Internet in a form — for example, HTML — that a browser can interpret and display.
It is aimed at creating a web site — a collection of files on one or more web servers — that presents content, including interactive features, to the end user in the form of web pages.

Web pages are usually classified as static or dynamic. A static page does not change its content or layout with every request. It stays the same until a human — a web master or a programmer — edits it by hand.

A dynamic page adapts its content or appearance to the situation: who the user is, what time it is, what the user clicks, or what has changed in the database. Content can change on the user's computer with client-side languages such as JavaScript, which modify the elements of the DOM.

Dynamic content can also be built on the server with server-side scripting languages such as PHP, Python, Java or ASP. The server runs the script, takes data from a database and sends ready HTML to the browser. Complex web applications usually combine both approaches.
As IT becomes more specialised, people often separate web design, which is about how pages look and feel, from web development, which covers the logic and infrastructure of all web services.

They are classified as static and dynamic. Static pages look the same for everyone until someone updates them manually. Dynamic pages change their content or appearance depending on the user, the time, the user's actions or data in a database.
On the client side — in the user's browser with JavaScript — and on the server side with languages like PHP, Python or Java. Complex applications usually use both.

A web site is a collection of information about a particular topic. Designing it means arranging and creating the web pages that make up the site. You can compare a web site to a book: every page of the book is a web page.

Because of the rapid development of the Internet, new design aspects appear all the time. For commercial sites, there are four basic aspects: content — useful information for the target audience; usability — a user-friendly interface and simple, reliable navigation; appearance — one consistent, professional style; and visibility — the site must be easy to find in search engines.

The first page of a site is called the home page or index. Some sites also have a splash page with a welcome message, a choice of language or a disclaimer. Today visitors are impatient, so splash pages are rarely used on commercial sites. Every page is a separate HTML file with its own URL, and all pages are connected by a menu of hyperlinks.

When the site is ready, it must be published: the web master uploads the files to a server, for example with an FTP client. To increase traffic, the site can be submitted to search engines, and the owner can exchange links with similar sites.
A web site is a collection of information about a particular topic, made up of web pages. It is compared to a book, where each page of the book is a web page.

Content — relevant information for the target audience; usability — a user-friendly site with simple, reliable navigation; appearance — a consistent, professional and appealing style; visibility — the site must be easy to find through major search engines and advertising.

Plan the site; create the pages (HTML files with their own URLs); link them with a navigation menu; publish (upload) the files to a server; promote the site: submit it to search engines, exchange links and create affiliations with similar sites.

Web site design combines several disciplines: information systems, information technology and communication design. A web site is an information system, and its parts are often classified as the front end and the back end.

The front end is everything the user can see and hear: the page layout, the user interface, graphics, text and audio. The back end is invisible: the organisation and efficiency of the source code, scripted functions and the server-side components that process the data sent from the front end.

In a small project, one multi-skilled person — a web master — can do everything. In a large project, a project manager organises collaborative work between specialists: designers, front-end and back-end developers, testers and content managers.

Components are divided into the front end — observable content such as layout, user interface, graphics, text and audio — and the back end — the organisation and efficiency of the source code, invisible scripted functions and server-side components that process the output from the front end.

Model answer: I would like to be a back-end developer because I enjoy logic, databases and algorithms more than visual design. / I prefer the front end because I like creating interfaces that people can see and use.
Accessibility means that everyone, including people with disabilities, can use a web site. To be accessible, web pages must follow several principles.

First, use semantic markup that gives the document a meaningful structure: headings, lists, paragraphs and navigation. Use a valid markup language that follows a published standard, a DTD or a Schema. Provide text equivalents for all non-text content, such as images and multimedia.

Second, write hyperlinks that make sense out of context, and avoid "Click here". Don't use frames, and use CSS rather than HTML tables for layout. Finally, write the page so that it stays clear when a screen reader reads the source code line by line. Tables used for design often turn into nonsense when they are read aloud.

The W3C allows one exception: layout tables are acceptable if they still make sense when they are linearized, or if an alternative version is available. Accessibility is also changing because of Content Management Systems, which let people edit pages without knowing a programming language.

Use semantic markup; use a valid markup language that conforms to a DTD or Schema; provide text equivalents for non-text content; write hyperlinks that make sense out of context; don't use frames; use CSS rather than tables for layout; make the page intelligible when a screen reader reads it line by line.
A screen reader reads the source code line by line. When tables are used for design, the reading order breaks and the information often becomes meaningless.

Before you create and upload a website, take time to plan exactly what it needs. The most important steps are to think about the audience, define the purpose and decide what content will be developed.

Purpose. A purpose statement shows what the site will accomplish and what users will get from it. Set short-term and long-term goals and measurable objectives, so that you can track progress and understand whether the site is successful.

Audience. The target audience is the group of people who are expected to visit the site. Make a list of their characteristics: who they are, what information they prefer, what computers and devices they use, and how experienced they are on the web.

Content. Collect all the necessary content and organise it according to the audience's needs. Remove anything that does not support the purpose. Test the content on a focus group, then group it into categories with short, descriptive titles. These titles become the links in your menu.

Compatibility and restrictions. Visitors use different browsers, screens and devices, so the compatibility of your site has limits. In the 2000s, Internet Explorer was the main restriction: it did not fully support W3C standards or PNG transparency. Many problems go unnoticed, so the only way to be sure is to test the site on each platform.

Purpose — what the site will accomplish, with short- and long-term goals and measurable objectives. Audience — who will visit and what they need: audience characteristics, information preferences, computer specifications and web experience. Content — collect, organise and categorise it, and remove anything that does not support the purpose. Compatibility and restrictions — browsers, screen resolution, image formats; test on every platform.
Model answer: The target audience is ISIP students aged 16–20 who study English for IT. They use smartphones and PCs, prefer short interactive tasks, and have good web experience.
As in any collaborative work, web designers do not always agree. They have different goals and different methods, and some debates have lasted for years. Here are a few of them.

Liquid versus fixed layouts. A liquid layout stretches to fill the browser window, while a fixed layout always has the same width. Proponents of liquid layouts say that they use the whole screen. Detractors answer that very long lines are hard to read. With a liquid layout, the designer relinquishes some control over how the page looks.

Flash. For years, Flash let designers create rich animations, but search engine crawlers could not read the text inside Flash, and users needed a plug-in. Some companies even banned it. The argument subsided only when HTML5 and CSS3 could do the same things without plug-ins.

CSS versus tables. Tables were created for tabular information, such as timetables or price lists. Using them for page layout subverts the meaning of HTML. Modern designers forgo table layouts and build pages from div blocks and CSS templates, even though every browser has its own quirks.

Form versus function. Some designers care most about beauty: fonts, colours and animation. Others care most about function: speed, clear lists with bullets, easy navigation. The best sites are synergistic: form and function work together and make each other stronger.
Model answer: I prefer a responsive layout, which combines both ideas. It is liquid on small screens and has a maximum width on large monitors, so lines stay easy to read.
Because HTML5, CSS3 and JavaScript made plug-ins unnecessary, mobile devices never supported Flash, and browsers finally banned it for security reasons.

Model answer: The intent of web design is to create sites with markup languages and tags. Pages can be static or dynamic. A site has a front end and a back end. Good commercial sites care about content, usability, appearance and visibility, and they must be accessible. Before building a site, we define its purpose, audience and content and check compatibility. Designers still argue about layouts, plug-ins, tables and the balance of form and function.
Hi everyone, and welcome to DevSpeak, the podcast about English for IT students. I'm Kate, and today my guest is Max, a second-year student who has just built his first real website. Hi, Max!
Hi, Kate! Thanks for inviting me.
So, tell us about the project. What kind of site did you build?
It's a website for a small pizza café near our college. At first, I made it completely static: just HTML and CSS files.
Static means that the pages don't change, right?
Exactly. A static page looks the same for every visitor until somebody edits the file by hand. And that was the problem. The owner changed the menu almost every week, and every time he called me.
So you became their full-time web master!
Pretty much! So I decided to make the menu dynamic. Now the dishes and prices are stored in a database, and a PHP script builds the page on the server for every request.
So the owner can update the menu himself?
Yes, through a simple admin form. He submits the new prices, and the site shows them immediately. No more phone calls at midnight.
Did you use any client-side scripting?
A little JavaScript. When you add a pizza to your order, the total price updates without reloading the page. The script changes the DOM right in the browser.
So you combined both approaches: server-side and client-side.
Right. I think most real projects do that.
What was the hardest part?
Honestly, the planning. I started coding before I understood the purpose of the site. Next time I'll define the audience and the content first.
Great advice. Thank you, Max! And thank you all for listening to DevSpeak. See you next time!
Welcome back to DevSpeak! Many students ask me the same question: should I go into front-end or back-end development? To answer it, I've invited Alex, a team lead at a web studio. Hello, Alex!
Hello, Kate. That's a great question to start with.
Let's begin with the basics. What is the front end?
The front end is everything the user can see and hear: the layout, the user interface, graphics, text and audio. Front-end developers work with HTML, CSS and JavaScript.
And the back end?

The back end is the invisible part. It's the source code, the scripts and the server-side components that process the data coming from the front end. For example, when you submit a login form, the back end checks your password.
Which one is more difficult?
Neither. They're just different. Front-end people need a good eye for design and patience with browser compatibility. Back-end people need to love logic, databases and security.
Can one person do both?

Yes, we call them full-stack developers. In a small project, one multi-skilled person can build the whole site. But in a big project, a project manager organises collaborative work between specialists.
What would you advise our students?
Try both. Build a small project from start to finish. You'll quickly feel what you enjoy more: making things look great or making things work fast.
And what about English?
It's essential. Documentation, error messages, Stack Overflow, code reviews: almost everything is in English. The better your English, the faster you grow.
Thanks, Alex! That's all for today. Keep coding and keep learning English!
Hi, and welcome to DevSpeak. Today we're talking about accessibility. My guest is Tom, a QA engineer who tests websites for accessibility. Tom, you also use a screen reader yourself, right?
That's right, Kate. I have very low vision, so I use a screen reader every day. It reads the page aloud, line by line.
What's the most common problem you meet?
Images without text equivalents. If a picture has no alt text, the screen reader just says "image", or it reads the file name, like "IMG underscore four thousand". That tells me nothing.
Not very helpful! What else?
Links that say "Click here". I often jump from link to link, so every link must make sense out of context. "Download the timetable" is great. "Click here" is useless.
Our textbook also says: don't use tables for layout.
Exactly. When a table is used for design, the reading order gets mixed up, and the information turns into nonsense. Use CSS for layout and keep tables for tabular information.
What about semantic markup?
It's my best friend. When a page has real headings, lists and a navigation element, I can jump straight to the part I need. Without them, I have to listen to the whole page.
Is accessibility only for people with disabilities?
Not at all. Captions help people in a noisy metro, good contrast helps on a sunny day, and a clear structure helps everyone, including search engines. Accessible sites are simply better sites.
Thank you, Tom. Listeners, check your projects today: add alt text and fix those "click here" links!
Welcome to DevSpeak! Last time, Max told us that he started coding too early. Today he's back to talk about planning. Hi, Max!
Hi, Kate! Yes, I've learned my lesson.
Your new client is a small fitness club, right? Where did you start this time?
With the purpose. I asked the owner: what should the website accomplish? She said she wanted more people to sign up for trial workouts. So that became our main goal.
Did you set measurable objectives?
Yes. Fifty new sign-ups a month through the site. That's a number we can track, so we'll know if the site is successful.
Nice. What about the audience?
We made a list of audience characteristics. Most visitors are between twenty and forty, they use smartphones, and they want three things: prices, the timetable and the address.
So you know their information preferences.
Exactly. And their computer specifications: mostly phones, so the site must be mobile-first.
How did you organise the content?

The owner gave me a lot of material: the history of the club, awards, fifty photos. We removed everything that didn't support the purpose. Then we grouped the rest into five categories: Prices, Timetable, Trainers, Trial Workout and Contacts. Those names became the menu links.
Did you test it?
We showed the prototype to a small focus group: five club members. They found the sign-up button in seconds. And, of course, I tested the site in different browsers and on different phones.
Plan first, code later. Thanks, Max! See you next week on DevSpeak.
Welcome to a special episode of DevSpeak: the great debates of web design! Alex is back with us. Hi, Alex!
Hi, Kate! I'm ready to argue.
Let's start with liquid versus fixed layouts. Which side were you on?
Years ago, I was a proponent of fixed layouts. I wanted full control. With a liquid layout, you relinquish some of that control: the page stretches, and the lines can get too long to read.
And now?
The debate has mostly subsided. We use responsive design: the layout is flexible, but it has a maximum width. In a way, both sides won.
Next: Flash. You worked with it, didn't you?

I did. Flash sites looked amazing, but they had serious problems. Search engine crawlers couldn't read the text inside, so nobody could find the sites. Users needed a plug-in, and it had security holes. Many companies banned it.
What about tables versus CSS?
Tables are perfect for tabular information, like a timetable. But using them for layout subverts the whole idea of HTML. Now we forgo table layouts and use divs, Flexbox and Grid.
Were there any quirks?
Oh, every browser had its own quirks! Internet Explorer was famous for them. We had to write special hacks just for it.
Last one: form or function?

Both! Beautiful fonts and colours mean nothing if the page is slow. But a fast page that looks terrible won't keep visitors either. The best designs are synergistic: form and function make each other stronger.
Great ending. Thanks, Alex, and thank you all for listening!
